nodes.silent: It doesn’t console. It says life is uncertain and asks you to do good while you can. It has no word for mourning someone, and nothing here is about ending your own life.

nodes.label: You want to walk away from it all
nodes.desc: You feel the pull to drop everything, and the Kural speaks both of letting go of attachment and of a home life rightly lived.
keywords: should i leave my family for a spiritual life
nodes.silent: It doesn’t settle this. One chapter praises letting go of attachment, another a home lived rightly, not one where you are hurt. Letting go there means a way of living, not an end to life. It has little for someone simply worn out.

nodes.label: It feels as if fate is against you
nodes.desc: Whatever you do seems to turn out badly, and the Kural holds two truths together, that nothing is stronger than fate and that those who strive without faltering will see its back.
keywords: why does this always happen to me
nodes.silent: It says nothing is stronger than fate, and also that those who don’t falter will see its back, and it leaves the two side by side. It has little for someone worn out. Its fate is about fortune, not about what someone else does to you.

nodes.label: Your kindness is not being returned
nodes.desc: You keep giving and get nothing back, and the Kural says help looks for no return, as no one repays the rain-cloud.
keywords: always giving and getting nothing back
taken for granted by people i help
nodes.silent: It doesn’t promise thanks, and it pulls two ways: help looks for no return, yet helping past what you have ruins you. It doesn’t say when to stop, and it has nothing for being used.

nodes.label: Someone helped you when you most needed it
nodes.desc: You owe a debt of help you can never repay, and the Kural says to hold it as huge however small it looks, and to remember it always.
keywords: a teacher who changed my life
nodes.silent: These lines are about what you feel you owe. They don’t say what a helper may ask of you, and they aren’t a reason to stay with someone who uses past help to control you.

nodes.label: Fire
nodes.desc: Fire as what burns and spreads, the measure of evil, of the tongue’s wound and of desire, from a spark in a straw stack to flames one can still sleep among.

nodes.label: The Rain-Cloud
nodes.desc: The cloud and its rain as the model of giving without return and of what all the world looks up to for life.

nodes.label: The Plough
nodes.desc: The plough and its work, standing for the labour all others rest on, and in the Tamil of Kural 872 used of bow and word as well.

nodes.label: The Elephant
nodes.desc: The great beast as strength under test, goaded, wounded, frightened by the tiger, mired in mud or decoyed by its own kind.

nodes.label: The Lamp
nodes.desc: The lamp or unfailing light that drives out dark, used of truth, wealth and family.

nodes.label: The Sea
nodes.desc: The sea as vastness, the ocean of births to be crossed and the depth of desire and grief.

nodes.label: The Boat
nodes.desc: The raft, boat or ship that carries one across or fails to, in Part 3 mostly the firmness that desire sweeps away.

nodes.label: The Moon
nodes.desc: The moon waxing and waning as friendship, spotted as a noble man's fault, and rivalled by the beloved's face.

nodes.label: The aṉiccam flower
nodes.desc: The tender aṉiccam, which fades at a breath, the Kural’s own measure of a guest’s heart and of the beloved’s softness.

nodes.label: Flowers
nodes.desc: Flowers as the beauty of eyes and face, and as what is delicate or unfulfilled, like learning that cannot be expounded.

nodes.label: The Tree
nodes.desc: Trees as what a person is to others, the fruit tree in the village, the medicine tree, the poison tree, the sapless tree, the thorn to fell while young.

nodes.label: Ripe Fruit
nodes.desc: Fruit ripe and unripe as the sweet and the harsh in speech and in love.

nodes.label: Seed and Sowing
nodes.desc: The seed and the sowing, by which deeds, desire and conduct bring their crop.

nodes.label: The Village Tank
nodes.desc: The tank and its channels as held wealth, full for all to draw on, or with its bunds gone and the water flowing away.

nodes.label: The Serpent
nodes.desc: The snake as deadly power close by, the cobra whose breath ends an army of rats and the cobra sharing one's hut.

nodes.label: The Eye
nodes.desc: The eye as what learning, spies and kindness are, so that one without them has only two sores in his head.

nodes.label: The Lover's Eyes
nodes.desc: The eyes in love as separate actors, battling, wounding, weeping and drying up, blamed for the pain they brought on.

nodes.label: The Ear
nodes.desc: The ear as a mouth to be fed and a treasure house, in which instruction is its food and its taste.

nodes.label: Toddy
nodes.desc: Toddy as desire’s rival and comparison, delighting only when drunk, where desire delights at a glance or a memory.

nodes.label: Ambrosia
nodes.desc: The food of immortality as the measure of what is sweetest, rain, a child's soup, the beloved's arms.

nodes.label: Cart and Axle
nodes.desc: The cart, the chariot and the axle pin, small things that bear or break under the load.

nodes.label: The Mountain
nodes.desc: The hill or mountain as stature and firmness, and as the safe height from which to watch a fight.

nodes.label: Earth the Bearer
nodes.desc: The earth as a patient woman who bears those who dig her, is burdened by the worthless and laughs at the idle.

nodes.label: The Sceptre
nodes.desc: The ruler's rod, straight or leaning, the visible sign of justice, to which the people look as to the rain-cloud.

nodes.label: Touchstone and Measuring Rod
nodes.desc: The touchstone, the rod and the balance by which worth, friends and minds are assayed.

nodes.label: Darkness
nodes.desc: Darkness as ignorance, the world of pain and the world seen without a smile, the state that light and insight end.

nodes.label: The File
nodes.desc: The iron file, that wears away power and a divided house, and that gives sharpness to wits with nothing behind them.

nodes.label: The Living Dead
nodes.desc: The one who breathes but is counted as a corpse, the Kural's verdict on those who lack what makes a life.

nodes.label: Bones
nodes.desc: Bone and skin as the bare body without loving-kindness, and the giving of one’s very bones to others.

nodes.label: Soul and Body
nodes.desc: The soul lodged in the body like a bird in a shell or a lodger in a borrowed room, used for life's frailty and for the closeness of lovers.

nodes.label: Disease
nodes.desc: Sickness as a figure, hunger as the evil disease, the spirit of strife as a malady, and love as what no other medicine cures.

nodes.label: The Ornament
nodes.desc: The jewel or ornament, a title the Kural gives to the virtue in question, modesty, sweet speech, considerateness or shame, over any real adornment.

nodes.label: The True Treasure
nodes.desc: The real wealth, the Kural’s recurrent claim that compassion, learning, desirelessness or listening is the treasure and that money is not.

nodes.label: The Sneeze
nodes.desc: The sneeze, taken to mean that someone is thinking of you, which Part 3 makes a comic proof of love and a cause of jealousy.

nodes.label: The Palmyra Stalk
nodes.desc: The palmyra stalk ridden in public by the lovelorn, a last resort of those torn from love that tramples all shame.

nodes.label: Millet and Palmyra
nodes.desc: The millet seed set against the palmyra tree, the Kural's pair for how small a thing may count as large.

nodes.label: Pallor
nodes.desc: The pale sallow colour that spreads over a woman parted from her lover, treated as an enemy, as his child and as a public proof.

nodes.label: Slipping Bracelets
nodes.desc: Bracelets slipping from an arm thinned by grief, which tell the world of the parting.

nodes.label: The Dream
nodes.desc: Dream as where absent lovers still meet, a comfort or a spite, which the waking state cuts short.

nodes.label: Evening
nodes.desc: Evening as the hour when love's grief peaks, advancing like an executioner on the woman left alone.

nodes.label: Night
nodes.desc: The long night of lovers, in which she alone is awake and which he wishes would last through the quarrel.

nodes.label: Tears
nodes.desc: Tears that proclaim love, that wear away a tyrant's wealth and that, in an enemy's eyes, cannot be trusted.

nodes.label: The Heart Addressed
nodes.desc: The heart spoken to as a second person, scolded, begged and sent as a messenger by one parted from love.

nodes.label: The Lord's Feet
nodes.desc: The holy feet to which one clings, the opening chapter's one image of refuge.

nodes.label: The Goddess of Fortune
nodes.desc: Lakshmi, who dwells with the hospitable and the diligent and leaves the envious to her elder sister Misfortune.

nodes.label: The God of Death
nodes.desc: Death as a person, who eats life, is beckoned by fools and faced by armies, and whom the lover meets in a woman's eyes.

nodes.label: Sword and Spear
nodes.desc: The blade and lance of the hero and the ruler, and the sword in a eunuch’s hand as the emblem of what cannot be used.

nodes.label: Bow and Arrow
nodes.desc: The bow and arrow, by whose shape a man's straightness is not to be judged and whose bending is a threat.

nodes.label: The watered plant
nodes.desc: A plant fed or starved at its root, the figure for what nourishes or kills spirit, counsel and love.

nodes.label: Beasts at their hour
nodes.desc: Birds and animals that win only at their moment or on their own ground, the figure for timing and place in strategy.

props.why: By god’s command rain keeps the world going, and with it righteousness, wealth and pleasure.
Those who renounce are the ones who show the world righteousness, wealth and pleasure as they truly are.
Of the three taught by those who renounce, only righteousness yields this life, the next and release, so it is stronger than the other two.
Home life is the first of the two states in which righteousness is done.
A wife is the companion of home life, so her worth is told next.
The last couplet of The Worth of a Wife named good children as the fine ornament of a home’s excellence, and that opened the way to this chapter.
Loving-kindness is fondness for the wife, the children and others joined to you, so it follows the chapters on them.
Only two people undivided in loving-kindness, working together, can care for guests.
Those who care for guests can’t do without sweet words.
For those who speak sweetly and keep to household righteousness, the one fault with no escape is destroying a kindness, and this guards against it.
Remembering a kindness can break your evenness towards the one who did it, and this says it must not break even there.
Restraint belongs to those impartial enough to see their own faults as they see a stranger’s.
Only those who have restrained body, speech and mind can keep good conduct.
Not wanting another man’s wife is found only in those who have good conduct.
He places it here to say that even those who have left the path and done wrong are to be borne.
Envy is not bearing what others have, the opposite of bearing wrongs, so it is forbidden here.
Beyond resenting what others have, even the thought of seizing it is a fault.
Faults of speech grow from faults of the mind, so backbiting follows envy and coveting.
Of the sins of speech a householder can give up, harsh words and backbiting have been dealt with, which leaves useless words.
After the sins of speech, this gathers up and forbids all the sins of the body.
What to avoid in mind, speech and body has been told, so this turns to what still remains to be done.
Giving looks to the next life, so it follows the duty to the world, which looks to this one.
Renown, this life’s reward for keeping household righteousness, comes mostly from giving.
Renunciation begins here, and compassion comes first because it matters to renunciation as loving-kindness does to home life.
Eating flesh is both cause and result of killing, so it can’t go with compassion and is forbidden here.
Austerity is taken up once refusing flesh has ripened your compassion for living things.
This forbids conduct that doesn’t fit austerity, when someone keeps the garb but lacks the strength and wants again the pleasures of desire they gave up.
The last chapter forbade faults over desire, and this one forbids faults over wealth.
Lying springs mostly from desire and wealth, so it follows the chapters on those two faults.
This forbids the anger that arises from lying.
Harm happens even without anger.
Not killing surpasses all the righteousness told so far and takes in what hasn’t been named, so it comes last.
Attachment to things won’t end until impermanence is understood, so this is told first.
Renunciation is letting go of attachment to wealth outside you and the body within, on seeing that neither lasts.
Knowing the truth, like renunciation, comes from holding to the one who has no attachment, so the two share one cause.
Old habit can still draw the mind back to the senses, and that thought, a seed of birth, is cut off by constant knowledge of the truth.
Fate is common to wealth and pleasure, so it can’t sit under either, and it is joined to righteousness, so it closes that part.
The Excellence of a Ruler opened this subject with “wakefulness, learning and resolve”, and this chapter expands it.
Praising learning wasn’t enough on its own, so it is shown from the other side as well.
Listening strengthens the understanding of those who have learned and gives it to those who haven’t.
This is having true understanding alongside the understanding that learning and listening give.
Only those with understanding can see these six as faults and remove them.
A ruler who has removed the six faults is fit to drive the cart of protection, and now takes those of great understanding as his helpers.
Petty company twists the mind and ruins both worlds, so joining it makes taking the great as allies useless.
Examining a task is done with the great, once keeping clear of petty company has made them useful allies.
A ruler who has weighed the means and settled on punishment now measures the four kinds of strength.
A ruler with the greater strength, setting out against his enemy, must next know the time that suits the march.
Knowing his strength and the time, a ruler setting out against his enemy must next know the ground where he can win.
Marching on an enemy with strength, time and ground known, a ruler needs this so that work gets done and no one betrays him.
Those a ruler has come to trust must now be employed in the tasks they can do.
Having told of those who do the ruler’s work, the book turns to the rest of his circle.
Kin are of use only where a ruler doesn’t lapse.
Justice can only be given by a ruler free of lapses.
The crooked sceptre is the opposite of the straight one.
Acts that frighten people belong with the crooked sceptre.
This sets out in full, for its importance, the kindly regard already spoken of in Not Ruling by Fear.
With the ruler’s own character told, the book turns to what he needs to run his land and take others’, and spies serve both, so they come first.
Whoever learns through spies what has happened must act on it, and can’t do that without drive.
Even those with drive can at times grow lazy through the pull of their nature.
Getting rid of laziness isn’t enough, because work is only carried out by effort.
Trouble comes to those who strive, whether from god, lack of wealth or strain on the body, and the mind must stay steady then.
The Minister said he must “speak with certainty”, and that matters so much that this chapter expands it.
Action must be good as well as speech.
Clean work needs firmness of mind if it is to be carried through to the end.
This is how a minister with that firmness carries out the work.
Making peace and making war, the two errands of an envoy, were treated above as ways of carrying out work.
The Envoy asked for “the qualities rulers desire”, so how to live with rulers comes next.
No one who lives close to rulers can do without this.
When you speak on business you need to know the assembly as well as read the ruler’s mind.
Having judged an assembly fit to speak before, you must speak to it without fear.
After the ruler and the minister comes the country they carry forward, which the other parts of the state, such as the fortress, can’t do without.
The fortress belongs to the country, yet it counts as a part of the state on its own, because it protects both country and ruler when enemies bring ruin.
Wealth is mostly made through the country and guarded by the fortress.
Wealth is what raises an army, and an army is what wins.
This is the surplus of valour in the army just described.
Friendship helps a ruler in his work as an army does.
You should befriend only those you have tested for the marks just given, so how to test them comes next.
Even tested friends have faults that can be borne, and fate too makes them err.
After faults that can be borne come faults that can’t, and friendship with such people must be dropped.
This is the second friendship to be dropped, the friendship of enemies who never join you at heart.
The book turns from friendship to enmity, which comes from anger and desire, and starts with folly, the first delusion at their root.
After folly comes the other delusion: to have a small understanding and rate it as great.
Of the anger and desire that come of delusion, anger weighs most with rulers, so what anger brings comes first, beginning with strife.
A ruler can’t be wholly without enemies, so the strife forbidden in general is prescribed here in one special case.
All that is weighed here concerns the enmity that isn’t worth having.
The enemy within is also among the enmities to be removed.
This was all that remained unsaid, so it closes the chapters on what anger brings.
What desire brings isn’t enmity outright, but it wrecks gain and brings ruin as enmity does, so it closes the part on enmity, starting here.
After the faults that come from a man’s own wife come those that come from women who sell their charms to anyone who pays.
In ruining conduct and understanding, liquor is like the women of the last chapter.
Like drinking, gambling and illness come between a person and righteousness, wealth and pleasure, and gambling comes first.
Illness, like gambling, comes between a person and righteousness, wealth and pleasure, so it is told next, with its medicine.
High birth is something all four varnas can’t do without, so the nature of those born to a high family comes first in this part.
Among the qualities of the well-born, honour comes first because it keeps their birth upright.
These good qualities, which lift you ever higher, arise only where you don’t fall from your standing.
This gathers up the many good qualities that don’t fall under greatness.
This is getting along with everyone, knowing their nature, without slipping yourself from greatness and worth.
The last couplet of Being Courteous said great wealth is of no use in someone without courtesy, and that opened this subject.
Raising your family belongs to those who feel shame at falling low.
Ploughing is the effort that the last chapter said raises a family.
The books of righteousness say the body, which can reach release, is to be kept even by begging that leaves honour whole, so this forbids Poverty’s utter renunciation.
After begging that leaves your honour whole comes the fear of begging that costs you your honour.
The base have none of the qualities stated or implied in all the chapters before, so they come after every one of them.
This happens the moment he first sees her, so it is told first.
A man struck by her beauty needs to read her signs if he is to reach her.
Having read her signs and come together with her, he speaks of his delight.
Praise of her beauty arises when he is delighting in their union.
Telling how great their love is arises from that union and that beauty.
Letting go of shame comes when love is at its height.
Telling of the gossip comes once shame has been given up.
Unable to bear the parting, she thinks always of her pain, and the thinking wastes her away.
Her eyes ache to see him once grief has wasted her.
Pallor comes when she can’t get to see him.
This grief belongs to the woman who has suffered pallor.
She saw the dream because she thought of him so much while awake.
Trusting the saying that no deed comes without a dream before it, she has borne the day, and evening’s grief belongs to such a woman.
Her features lose their beauty when grief is at its height.
This comes once her features have lost their beauty and she has nothing left to hold on to.
Her reserve breaks down because she has spoken to her heart.
Her words here come from her lost reserve.
This happens once he has come back and they are together.
She has made known his intent to leave, yet the eagerness isn’t his alone: her great longing makes it rise in her too.
Her heart, hurrying to union, won’t think of sulking even with cause, so she sulks with her heart, and he with his.
When neither heart hurries to union and both mean to sulk, the two sulk with each other.
She has no cause to sulk, but her love runs so high that she imagines a fine cause and lays it on him.
When a sulk like that has made union sweeter, each of them delights in the sulking.

props.quote: People with it would give even their bones for others

props.quote: everything that should hurt can turn out well

props.quote: can enjoy only what fate has allotted

props.why: Asks why someone who welcomes good times should be distressed by bad ones.
props.quote: why be distressed when the bad ones come

props.why: Asks someone with bad fortune to meet it as they met good.
props.quote: If you welcome good times as good

props.quote: What is stronger than fate?

props.quote: Loving-kindness makes you warm towards people, and that warmth brings friendship

props.quote: The fate that brings you wealth also brings the drive to work

props.why: The fate that takes wealth away brings laziness.
props.quote: The fate that takes it away brings laziness

props.why: Fate that is bringing gain widens the mind.
props.quote: Fate that is bringing you gain widens your mind

props.quote: the world begins with the First Lord

props.why: Says all study is wasted unless it ends in worship.
props.quote: worship the good feet

props.quote: the one whose knowledge is pure

props.why: Worship at the feet stands for all devotion, the only real return on learning.
props.quote: the good feet

props.quote: will live long on the earth

props.why: The feet of the one who walked on the flower are the place to reach.
props.quote: the noble feet

props.why: Says those who reach his feet will never suffer.
props.quote: will have no suffering, ever

props.why: Praises him as one who wants nothing and rejects nothing.
props.quote: the one who wants nothing and rejects nothing

props.why: Reaching the feet is what puts people beyond suffering.
props.quote: reach the feet

props.quote: the great sea of births

props.why: The Lord's feet are the only hold that brings anyone across.
props.quote: the Lord’s feet

props.quote: the world keeps going

props.quote: rain should be known as ambrosia

props.quote: Rain makes good food

props.quote: hunger will settle in the wide world

props.quote: If the riches called rain run short

props.quote: conduct can’t go on without rain

props.quote: those who renounce while holding to right conduct

props.quote: stands above all else

props.why: Those who renounce are named outright and declared beyond all counting.
props.quote: the greatness of those who renounce

props.quote: like counting all who have died on earth

props.quote: those who have weighed the two

props.why: The greatness of those who chose this path is what shines out in the world.
props.quote: shines out in the world

props.quote: guards the five senses

props.quote: the strength of one who quenched the five senses

props.quote: Those who do what is hard to do are great

props.why: Those whose speech comes true are, in this chapter, those who renounce.
props.quote: people whose speech comes true

props.quote: The anger of those who stand on the hill called virtue

props.quote: the hill called virtue

props.why: Takes the title of sage and gives it to those who have earned it by tenderness.
props.quote: Those called sages

props.why: Makes tenderness towards all life the reason anyone deserves the name.
props.quote: tenderness towards every living thing

props.why: Asks what could pay better than the one thing that brings both distinction and wealth.
props.quote: What gain could be greater for a living being?

props.quote: no ruin greater than forgetting it

props.quote: never stopping, do righteous deeds

props.quote: To be without stain in your mind

props.quote: the companion that doesn’t die when you die

props.quote: From each thing you have let go of, you suffer no more pain

props.why: Tells someone drawn to letting go that every single thing dropped is a sorrow escaped.
props.quote: each thing you have let go of

props.quote: renounce while you can

props.quote: crush the hold of the five senses

props.why: Asks for more than the senses: everything you wanted is to go, all together.
props.quote: give up, all together, everything you wanted

props.quote: Owning even one thing brings back delusion

props.quote: Those who renounce completely have arrived

props.quote: Otherwise you will see impermanence

props.quote: The moment attachment ends, birth is cut off

props.why: Blames a wretched birth on one error, taking what isn’t real for what is.
props.quote: the delusion that takes what isn’t real for what is

props.why: Shows what its removal yields: those rid of it get joy in place of darkness.
props.quote: have left delusion behind

props.why: Credits stainless seeing with bringing joy to the one who has it.
props.quote: see without stain

props.why: Error is a darkness here, and it lifts for the one who sees clearly.
props.quote: darkness goes and joy comes

props.why: Puts heaven nearer than earth for those whose doubts have ended.
props.quote: heaven is nearer than the earth

props.why: Counts even mastery of the senses as no gain without knowledge of the truth.
props.quote: no gain in it without knowledge of the truth

props.why: Names the work of understanding as finding the true in every thing, whatever form it takes.
props.quote: understanding is seeing the reality in it

props.why: Joins learning to insight and rewards the pair with a path that doesn’t come back.
props.quote: Those who learn here and see the truth

props.why: Makes the path with no return to this world the prize held out.
props.quote: the path that doesn’t come back here

props.why: Relieves the one who has reasoned their way to what truly is of all thought of another birth.
props.quote: you need not think of being born again

props.why: Gives understanding its aim: to see the pure reality called excellence.
props.quote: see the pure reality called excellence

props.why: Birth itself is the folly here, and ending it is what understanding aims at.
props.quote: the folly called birth

props.why: Treats living so that attachment dies as what sends future ills away.
props.quote: live so that attachment dies

props.why: Knowing what to rest on is this insight, and it comes before the living.
props.quote: If you know what to rest on

props.why: Heads the three whose going takes pain along with it.
props.quote: desire

props.why: Stands between desire and delusion among the three whose names must go for pain to go.
props.quote: anger

props.why: Closes the list of three, the mistaking of things that goes with wanting and rage.
props.quote: delusion

props.why: Says what craving is at bottom: the seed from which every life’s births are grown.
props.quote: craving is the seed

props.why: Birth is what never ends, and craving is the seed it grows from.
props.quote: the seed that yields

props.why: Names it the one longing worth having, if one must long at all.
props.quote: want not to be born

props.why: Gives the paradox: what opens the way is wanting to want nothing.
props.quote: wanting to want nothing

props.why: No wealth here, and nothing anywhere else, comes up to it.
props.quote: no great wealth here to match wanting nothing

props.why: Takes the word wealth from money and hands it to the state of wanting nothing.
props.quote: no great wealth here

props.why: Reduces purity to one thing, having no craving left.
props.quote: Purity is having no craving

props.why: Keeps the name of free for those rid of craving and denies it to the rest.
props.quote: Those who are called free are the ones free of craving

props.why: Shows everyone else as not free in the same way, for lack of it.
props.quote: The others are not free in the same way

props.quote: Craving is what deceives you

also.why: Craving works by deceiving you, so fearing it is called righteousness.
also.quote: Craving is what deceives you

props.why: Says that with craving wholly cut away, deeds that never fail come as you want them.
props.quote: cut off craving completely

props.why: Piles suffering on suffering upon whoever goes on craving.
props.quote: suffering comes on and on, without end

props.why: Shows a person always after the next thing that the wanting itself feeds the misery.
props.quote: Those without craving have no suffering

props.why: Calls it outright the worst suffering of all.
props.quote: craving, the worst suffering of all

also.why: Craving is itself called the worst suffering, not just a cause of it.
also.quote: craving, the worst suffering of all

props.why: Offers unbroken joy, and not later but here, to whoever destroys craving.
props.quote: joy goes on unbroken, even here

props.why: Declares it a hunger that no getting can ever fill.
props.quote: whose nature is never to be filled

also.why: However much it gets, craving stays unfilled, because that is its nature.
also.quote: whose nature is never to be filled

props.why: Tells someone stuck chasing more that satisfaction lies in stopping, not in the next gain.
props.quote: If you give up craving

props.quote: resolve

props.why: Asks that a ruler be easy for people to see.

props.why: Names a sharp tongue as the other thing an esteemed ruler must not have.

props.quote: easy to see and not harsh in speech

props.quote: The world rests under the umbrella

props.why: Calls it a virtue in a ruler to sit still under what is bitter to hear.

props.why: Holds up the ruler with all these gifts as the brightest of his kind.
props.quote: a light among rulers

props.why: Giving leads the list of what makes a light among rulers.
props.quote: Giving

props.why: The straight sceptre, the Tamil’s செங்கோல், is third of the four.

props.quote: two sores on their faces

props.why: Rebukes her heart as a useless accomplice that rushes to him without the agreed sulk.
props.quote: You won’t sulk first and enjoy him after.

props.why: Shows the fear outlasting success: to have him at last is only to start dreading his loss.
props.quote: when it has him it fears parting

also.why: Even having him brings no rest. Her heart simply moves from one fear to the other.
also.quote: when it has him it fears parting

props.why: Turns on her heart as a worthless thing whose only skill is gnawing at her.
props.quote: only to eat me up

props.why: Blames her fall on bad company, and the company is her own heart.
props.quote: Caught up with this worthless, foolish heart

props.why: The maid urges a sulk for the sport of seeing him suffer a little.
props.quote: Sulk, and let us see

props.why: Playful counsel to the woman herself on how to receive him.
props.quote: Don’t embrace him.

props.why: Says what the sulk is: the seasoning of union, good only in small measure.
props.quote: A sulk is like the right amount of salt.

props.why: Gives a working rule for any tiff: a little does no harm, so do not drag it out.
props.quote: Drawing it out is like a little too much.

props.why: Said to the man’s face: leaving a sulking woman unembraced adds to her pain.
props.quote: Not to embrace those who sulk with you

props.why: Warns against leaving a quarrel open: it hurts someone who is hurting already.
props.quote: like bringing fresh pain to people already in distress

props.why: Shows what refusing to make up does: it cuts at the root of something already withering.
props.quote: cutting a withered creeper at the root

props.why: Leaving someone’s sulk unsoothed cuts at the root a creeper already withered.
props.quote: cutting a withered creeper at the root

props.why: Grants the sulk a grace that adorns even those of fine character.
props.quote: What graces those of fine character

props.why: Treats deep and light sulks as what desire can’t do without.
props.quote: Without the deep sulk and the light one

props.why: Desire without sulking is fruit gone past its best, or fruit too green to eat.
props.quote: a fruit too ripe and a fruit too green

props.why: Finds the one true pain inside the game: not knowing how far off the making-up is.
props.quote: There is a pain even in sulking

also.why: Even the pleasure of a sulk has its pain: what if coming together is delayed?
also.quote: There is a pain even in sulking

props.why: Sets its test: a sulk is sweet only with those who love you.
props.quote: sulking is sweet with those who love you

also.why: A sulk is sweet only with someone who loves you, as water is sweet in the shade.
also.quote: sulking is sweet with those who love you

props.why: Brands his own yearning for a woman who leaves a sulk to wither as mere craving.
props.quote: That is only craving.

props.why: Refuses his embrace because, she says, every woman’s eyes have already had their share of him.
props.quote: eat you up with their eyes

also.why: She refuses him because every woman’s eyes have had their share of him.
also.quote: I won’t go near your chest, you philanderer

props.why: Flung directly at him, with “philanderer” as the taunt.
props.quote: you philanderer

props.why: His sneeze is a ruse to force a blessing from a woman refusing to speak.
props.quote: He knew I would say, “Live long.”

props.why: A flower is enough: her suspicion turns it into proof of another woman.
props.quote: You wear it to show some woman

also.why: Any flower he wears becomes proof, to her, of some other woman.
also.quote: You wear it to show some woman

props.why: A vow of love is heard as an admission that there are others to compare her with.
props.quote: Than who? Than who?

also.why: His “more than anyone” only makes her ask who the others are.
also.quote: she sulked: “Than who? Than who?”

props.why: Finds a sulk in a tender remark: to have remembered her, she says, is to have forgotten her.
props.quote: So why did you forget me?

props.why: Her blessing turns to tears the moment she wonders who else has him in mind.
props.quote: Who was thinking of you, that you sneezed?

also.why: She blesses his sneeze, then takes it back and weeps at who might be thinking of him.
also.quote: Who was thinking of you, that you sneezed

props.why: A sneeze, the sign of being remembered, becomes evidence of a rival.
props.quote: I sneezed and she blessed me.

props.why: Now it is the concealing that offends, so nothing he does can clear him.
props.quote: Are you hiding from me

also.why: When he holds back a sneeze, she weeps at what he must be hiding.
also.quote: Are you hiding from me

props.why: The stifled sneeze springs the trap that the open one had set.
props.quote: I held back a sneeze

props.why: His very skill at soothing her is taken as proof that there have been others.
props.quote: So this is how you are with others too.

also.why: His soothing her becomes proof of how he must be with others.
also.quote: So this is how you are with others too

props.why: Even rapt admiration of her own beauty is suspected of a hidden comparison.
props.quote: Who are you thinking of, looking at all of me like that?

also.why: Even his quiet gaze is read as thinking of someone else.
also.quote: Who are you thinking of

props.why: She sulks at a faultless man for the tenderness it draws out of him.
props.quote: sulking is what draws out his tenderness

props.why: Counts the small hurt of sulking as worth it, since his tenderness comes back greater.
props.quote: The small hurt of sulking

props.why: Asks whether heaven itself can beat it, so long as the pair are truly one.
props.quote: Is there any heaven better than a lovers’ quarrel

props.why: The quarrel carries its own undoing: inside it is the weapon that breaks her resolve.
props.quote: is the weapon that breaks my resolve

props.why: Being kept from her soft shoulders is the sulk’s gesture, and even the innocent party finds pleasure in it.
props.quote: being kept from the soft shoulders of the one you love has a pleasure of its own

props.why: Ranks the quarrel above the embrace, as a meal well settled above the eating of it.
props.quote: a quarrel is sweeter than making love

props.why: Settles who comes out ahead in a lovers’ quarrel: the one who loses has won.
props.quote: the one who loses has won

props.why: Hopes another quarrel will bring back the sweetness of their lovemaking.
props.quote: Will a quarrel bring back the sweetness of our lovemaking

props.why: He wants more of her sulking, and is in no hurry for it to end.
props.quote: Let her go on sulking

props.why: Night is begged to stay, so that the sweet quarrel can run on.
props.quote: let the night run on while I plead

props.why: The book’s last word on the sulk: it is the joy of desire.
props.quote: Sulking is the joy of desire

also.why: Sulking is the joy of desire, and its own joy is the embrace that ends it.
also.quote: the joy of sulking is the embrace that ends it

props.why: Sets the embrace of reconciliation above even the sweetness of the quarrel.
props.quote: the joy of sulking is the embrace that ends it

props.why: She tells her heart that desire and modesty can’t both be borne: one has to go.
props.quote: give up desire or give up modesty

props.why: Desire’s axe breaks the door, and modesty’s bolt gives way with it.
props.quote: The axe of desire breaks down the door of reserve, bolted with modesty

props.why: Desire leaves no room to sulk: every attempt at it collapses the moment he is near.
props.quote: I went off meaning to sulk. I saw my heart was ready to join him

props.why: A sulk has its sweetness only with those who love you, as water has its sweetness in the shade.
props.quote: sulking is sweet with those who love you

props.why: Without sulks deep and light, desire is fruit too ripe or too green.
props.quote: Without the deep sulk and the light one, desire is like a fruit too ripe and a fruit too green.

props.why: The sulk closes in an embrace, and that embrace is its whole sweetness.
props.quote: the joy of sulking is the embrace that ends it

props.why: Fate gets there before any plan to beat it, yet those who strive without faltering are promised they will see its back.
props.quote: What is stronger than fate? … will see the back of fate itself

props.why: What fate denies won’t stay however you guard it, yet effort pays the wages of your toil even if god won’t allow it.
props.quote: What isn’t yours by fate won’t stay … Even if god won’t allow it, effort pays the wages

props.why: The fate that takes wealth away brings laziness, yet making no effort is called your own disgrace, not fate’s.
props.quote: The fate that takes it away brings laziness … The disgrace is to know what must be known and make no effort

props.why: Austerity is striven for because it brings what you want as you want it, yet craving can never be filled and is to be given up.
props.quote: what you want comes as you want it … If you give up craving, whose nature is never to be filled

props.why: The highest wisdom does no evil even to those who hate you, yet austerity is held out as a power that can crush enemies, if you wish it.
props.quote: do no evil even to those who hate you … Crushing enemies and raising those who are dear: if you wish it, austerity can do both

props.why: Those on the hill called virtue have an anger hard to withstand, yet renouncing anger is what makes you the equal of renouncers.
props.quote: The anger of those who stand on the hill called virtue is hard to withstand … Those who renounce anger are the equals of renouncers

props.why: Think how you stand before the strong before you go against the weak, says one; the other tells you to seek enmity with the weak without holding back.
props.quote: When you go against those weaker than you, think of yourself before those stronger … Without holding back, seek enmity with the weak

props.why: Someone who prizes anger will surely be ruined, yet the wise are shown burning within and watching for their time.
props.quote: Someone who prizes anger will be ruined … They watch for the time and burn within

props.why: Uprightness and shame come by nature only to those of good family, yet birth is the same for all and only what they do sets them apart.
props.quote: Only in those born of a good family do uprightness and shame come together by nature … Birth is the same for every living being

props.why: No one is crueller than those who live by deceit as if they had renounced, yet a spy is praised for taking that very form.
props.quote: those who don’t renounce in their hearts but live by deceit, as if they had renounced … A spy takes the form of those who have renounced

props.why: A heart free of falsehood wins every heart, yet with a foe you cannot yet break from, you are told to feign friendship.
props.quote: Live without lying in your heart … be friends with the face, and put friendship out of the heart

props.why: Nothing at all is better than truthfulness, says one, yet the other ranks not killing first and puts not lying second.
props.quote: nothing at all is better than truthfulness … Not killing stands alone as good. Next after it, not lying is good

props.why: Compassion is the wealth above all wealth, and goods are found even among the low, yet compassion is said to thrive with wealth as its foster-mother.
props.quote: The wealth of compassion is the wealth among wealth … thrives with the rich foster-mother called wealth

props.why: Wealth by its nature doesn’t stay, yet it is also called an unfailing lamp that goes to whatever land you think of.
props.quote: It is the nature of wealth not to stay … The unfailing lamp called wealth

props.why: The one who lives home life well is first among all who strive, yet those who renounce completely have arrived and all others are caught in a net.
props.quote: The one who lives home life as it should be lived is first among all who strive … All others are deluded, and caught in a net

props.why: Ruin from helping others is worth buying, even if you must sell up, yet you are also told to give knowing your limit and to look after your wealth.
props.quote: that ruin is worth buying, even if you must sell up to do it … Give in the right way, knowing your limit

props.why: Not killing is what righteous action is, yet a ruler who punishes the wicked with death is likened to someone pulling weeds from a green crop.
props.quote: What is righteous action? Not killing … A ruler who punishes the wicked with death is like someone pulling weeds from a green crop

props.why: Begging from those who hide nothing is like giving, says one chapter; the next says not begging is worth ten million times more, even there.
props.quote: Begging is like giving … not begging is worth ten million times more

props.why: Without people who beg the world would be a wooden puppet; the next chapter curses its maker if anyone must live by begging.
props.quote: Without people who beg, this great cool world would be a wooden puppet … wanted people to live even by begging, let him wander far and perish

props.why: A lack of understanding is called the worst poverty and no other lack counts, yet the other answers that only poverty hurts like poverty.
props.quote: The world does not count any other lack as poverty … Only poverty hurts like poverty

props.why: Those of an old family keep their good nature when their means shrink, yet poverty brings even them a weakness from which shameful words are born.
props.quote: those of an old family don’t part from their good nature … Even in those of good family, poverty brings a weakness

props.why: Only killing the good done to you leaves no escape, says one; the other says no one escapes their own deed, which follows them and kills.
props.quote: Those who have killed any good may still escape … The enemy that is your own deed never goes away

props.why: A single evil word turns all your good bad, yet the noble may say things without goodness, so long as they say nothing useless.
props.quote: If a single evil word does its harm, the good you have done turns bad … Let the noble say things without goodness if they will

props.why: The one at a ruler’s side must tell him what is good for him, however he takes it, yet those around him are told to say what isn’t disliked, and to please.
props.quote: it is the duty of the one at his side to tell him what is good for him … say what is needed and not disliked, in a way that pleases

props.why: Desire grown full leaves no room for a sulk, she says; he says sulking is sweet with those who love you.
props.quote: you must not sulk even by a millet seed … sulking is sweet with those who love you

props.why: Remembering their days together is how she stays alive, yet keeping him in her heart, she says later, will only cost her more of her beauty.
props.quote: I live by remembering the days I was with him … If we keep in our heart the one who left us and won’t come near, we will lose still more of our beauty

props.why: Doting on a wife bars a man from the finest reward, yet the lover asks if even the world of the lotus-eyed one is sweeter than her shoulders.
props.quote: Men who dote on their wives won’t win the finest reward … Is the world of the lotus-eyed one sweeter than sleep on the soft shoulders of the one you love?

props.why: Many who didn’t know their strength broke halfway, yet all your thoughts are to be of rising higher, since even failing has the nature of not failing.
props.quote: set out on a surge of zeal and broke halfway … Let all your thoughts be of rising higher

props.why: The wise won’t accept an unlearned man’s cleverness even when it is very good, yet understanding is seeing the reality in what you hear, from anyone.
props.quote: Even when an unlearned man’s cleverness is very good, the wise don’t accept it … Whatever you hear, from whoever’s mouth, understanding is seeing the reality in it

props.why: For those who hold to friendship there is no leaving it once made, yet with those who spoil your work you are told to let it slowly slip away.
props.quote: once made there is no leaving it … let the friendship slowly slip away

props.why: People can be red outside and black inside, yet the face, like crystal, is said to show what is strongest in the heart.
props.quote: red outside like the crab’s-eye seed, yet black inside … the face shows what is strongest in the heart

props.why: The enmity of a man who does a task all wrong is worth paying for, yet the very next chapter says no one should want enmity, even in jest.
props.quote: Even if you must pay for it, be sure to get the enmity … No one should want it, even in jest

props.why: The sceptre, not the spear, brings a ruler victory, yet an army that fears no wound and wins is ranked first of all his riches.
props.quote: It is not the spear that brings a ruler victory. It is the sceptre … A complete army that fears no wound and wins is the first of all a ruler’s riches

props.why: Doubting someone you have come to trust brings endless suffering, yet a spy is there to watch everyone alike, even those who do your work and your kin.
props.quote: to doubt someone you have come to trust … those who do your work, your own kin

props.why: Learning lifts you above others as humans stand above beasts, unless you fear an assembly of the good, when you sink below the unlearned.
props.quote: those who have learned and understood, yet fear an assembly of the good, are lower than the unlearned … As beasts are to humans, so others are to those who have learned bright books

props.why: Learning alone doesn’t set you above the rest: someone who studies, teaches and still has no self-control is the greatest fool of all.
props.quote: No one is a greater fool than someone who studies, understands, teaches others, and still has no self-control … As beasts are to humans, so others are to those who have learned bright books

props.why: Bearing with those who scorn you is called the highest thing, but holding back anger only counts where the anger could take effect.
props.quote: Whoever holds back anger where it can take effect truly holds it back … the highest thing is to bear with those who scorn you

props.why: Humility is called good in everyone, but bowing low belongs to plenty: when your means shrink, you are told to stand tall.
props.quote: In plenty, bow low. When your means shrink, stand tall … Humility is good in everyone

props.why: Doing good however you can isn’t enough: even good can go wrong if it isn’t done knowing each person’s nature.
props.quote: Even doing good can go wrong, if you don’t do it knowing each person’s nature … do righteous deeds everywhere they can be done

props.why: Sulking may be the joy of desire, but it is like salt: drawing it out is a little too much.
props.quote: Drawing it out is like a little too much … Sulking is the joy of desire

props.why: Renown is made the point of appearing at all, but those who want glory with strength of character won’t do anything unworthy even for glory.
props.quote: won’t do anything unworthy, even for glory … If you appear, appear with renown

props.why: Only kin are said to cherish old ties when you have lost everything, but an enemy within who is close by kinship brings harms that lead towards death.
props.quote: When an enemy within appears who is close by kinship, it brings many harms … Only kin go on cherishing old ties even when you have lost everything

props.why: Trust is to go to those who pass every test, but many who pass every test still change once they are doing the work.
props.quote: many people change with the nature of the work … Test someone by these four, righteousness, wealth, pleasure and fear for their life, and then trust them

props.why: The rule to act only after careful deliberation has an exception: when a rare chance comes, do not hesitate.
props.quote: do at that very moment what is hard to do … Think, then commit to the task

props.why: A ruler’s honour must never slip from valour, but honour that has lost its nobility is itself counted among a ruler’s faults.
props.quote: honour that has lost its nobility … an honour that never slips from valour

props.why: Wanting nothing is set above everything: a pride that breeds victory in one, a wealth with no equal here or there in the other.
props.quote: The pride of wanting nothing breeds victory … There is no great wealth here to match wanting nothing

props.why: A family’s rise rests on refusing to idle, put as treating laziness for what it is in one and as not resting your hands from the work in the other.
props.quote: should treat laziness as the laziness it is … I won’t rest my hands from the work

props.why: Answer those who harm you by outdoing them in goodness: defeat them by your own worth, or punish them with good that shames them.
props.quote: Defeat by your own worth those who wrong you … do them such good that they are ashamed

props.why: Good done to the one who harmed you is the answer in each, and the later couplet makes it the very test of worth.
props.quote: do them such good that they are ashamed … What use is worth, if you don’t do kindness even to those who have done you harm?

props.why: Deliberate injury is no licence: even when someone hurts you out of hate or to pick a quarrel, you do not return it.
props.quote: Not harming in return, even when someone has harmed you in hatred … it is best not to answer with harm out of strife

props.why: However great the wrong, even one that burns like many fires, the good course is the same: do not be moved to answer it.
props.quote: it is good to suffer the pain and do nothing unrighteous … it is good not to be angry, if you can

props.why: No necessity excuses a shameful act, not a hungry mother in one nor things you can’t do without in the other.
props.quote: Even if you see the mother who bore you go hungry, don’t do what the worthy condemn … Even things you can’t do without, give them up if they would lower you

props.why: Anyone who wants to be free of suffering has the same single course in each: do no harm, since harm returns to its doer.
props.quote: If you don’t want painful things to strike you down, don’t do evil things to others … Those who want to be free of pain cause none

props.why: Evil comes back to those who do it, unprompted: it stays at their feet like a shadow in one and arrives by afternoon, by itself, in the other.
props.quote: like a shadow that never leaves, and stays at their feet … harm will come to you in the afternoon, by itself

props.why: Turn on your own faults the eye you keep for others’ and no harm can reach you, said first to everyone and later to the ruler.
props.quote: If you could see your own faults as you see strangers’ faults … If a ruler removes his own faults first, and then looks at those of others

props.why: A high aim that fails beats a low one that succeeds: rising thoughts don’t truly fail, and a spear that missed an elephant outdoes an arrow in a hare.
props.quote: Even when it fails, it has the nature of not failing … Better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that hit a hare

props.why: You can get what you have set your mind on, on one condition stated in each: that you keep your mind on it and stay firm.
props.quote: Getting what you have set your mind on is easy, if you can keep your mind on it … Those who plan will get what they planned, just as they planned it, if they are firm

props.why: What you offer those who can’t take it is simply lost: ambrosia spilled in a filthy yard, or a lesson that leaves the teacher seeing nothing himself.
props.quote: like ambrosia spilled in a filthy yard … Whoever tries to show a man who can’t see ends up seeing nothing himself

props.why: A fort is only as good as those in it: there is no fort for those who are afraid, and none for those with no excellence in action.
props.quote: There is no fort for those who are afraid … with those who have no excellence in action it is no fortress

props.why: A fortress is not only the refuge of the weak: the strong and powerful, each insists, gain just as much from one.
props.quote: Even to the strong and warlike, a gain that rests on a stronghold brings many benefits … A fortress is of value to those who are strong

props.why: Learning that cannot be put across to others is worthless: a flower without scent in one, good for nothing in the other.
props.quote: like flowers that bloom in clusters but have no scent … of no use, however much they have learned

props.why: The person worth having is described in nearly the same words, well-born and dreading blame, first as one to trust and then as a friend.
props.quote: born of good family, free of faults, and has the shame that dreads a scar … Someone well-born, who shrinks from blame upon himself

props.why: Rule stays sound only if the ruler looks into it daily: do so every day, or watch the land go to ruin day by day.
props.quote: Let the ruler look into it every day … When a ruler doesn’t look into things daily and do justice, his land goes to ruin day by day

props.why: Looks are no measure of a person, shown by the cruel arrow and the bent harp in one and by the axle pin of a great chariot in the other.
props.quote: Judge people the same way, by what they do … Don’t scorn people for how they look

props.why: No prize justifies a stain on your name: not piled-up millions for those of good family, not the wide world for the best of people.
props.quote: Even for piled-up millions, those of good family won’t do anything that lowers them … won’t want the wide world unless they have shame as their fence

props.why: Gain made the wrong way is to be let go, however good it looks: give it up at once in one, let it roll away in the other.
props.quote: let go at once of gain that comes from leaving the middle … don’t embrace it, let it roll away

props.why: Wealth won by stealing or deceit can’t hold, however it seems to grow: it perishes in one, and it is water in a pot of raw clay in the other.
props.quote: seems to grow, then perishes beyond all measure … like pouring water into a pot of raw clay

props.why: Failing to guard in advance is punished when the blow comes: you are straw before a fire in one, and left regretting it in the other.
props.quote: like a stack of straw before a fire … will regret that mistake when the blow lands

props.why: Giving trust or friendship without testing is the same mistake with a lasting price: suffering for those after you, or a sorrow that kills.
props.quote: Trust a stranger without testing them, and the suffering won’t end … Someone who makes a friend without looking and looking again ends in a sorrow that kills him

props.why: Desire outdoes liquor in the same way, heard first from him and then from her: liquor must be drunk, but desire delights at a glance.
props.quote: It can’t delight those who merely see, as desire does … toddy can’t do this, but desire can

props.why: She answers the same village gossip twice: they say he has left her, but they cannot see him in her heart or in her dreams.
props.quote: This town says he lives apart from me … They say he left me in waking life

props.why: What a service is worth lies not in the act but in the person it reaches: the worth of the guest in one, of those who received it in the other.
props.quote: It is measured by the worth of the guest … It is the worth of those who received it

props.why: Her reserve does not save her: desire breaks out of hiding into the open, whatever she had prided herself on.
props.quote: It breaks out of hiding into the open … Now my desire has gone past hiding, out into the public square

props.why: Nothing, each declares, is greater than a woman holding firm, whether in chastity or in not riding the palmyra stalk under a sea of desire.
props.quote: What is greater than a woman, if she has the strength called chastity? … Nothing is greater than a woman

props.why: The joy of desire is a sequence, not a state: the sulk first, then the embrace that ends it.
props.quote: Sulking, making up and coming together … the joy of sulking is the embrace that ends it

props.why: Losing a fool as a friend is a gain: plain gain in one and, with irony, very sweet in the other, because the end brings no pain.
props.quote: to give up the friendship of fools and get clear of them … When it ends, it brings no pain at all

props.why: She tells the same small defeat twice: she set out to sulk, and her heart had already gone to him.
props.quote: I went off meaning to sulk. I saw my heart was ready to join him … I went there to sulk, my friend, but my heart forgot that and went to join him

props.why: Where anger can take effect nothing is worse, says one, yet the other declares the carelessness of great delight worse than boundless rage.
props.quote: Where it can, nothing is worse … Worse than boundless rage is the carelessness

props.why: Anger is wrong even when you cannot strike, yet the wise are praised for keeping theirs alive until they can.
props.quote: Anger is bad where it can’t take effect … They watch for the time and burn within

props.why: Ruin from helping others is worth buying, even if you must sell up, yet helping without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth.
props.quote: that ruin is worth buying, even if you must sell up to do it … Helping others without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth

props.why: What fate makes yours won’t leave even if you throw it out, yet helping others without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth.
props.quote: What is yours won’t leave, even if you throw it out … Helping others without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth

props.why: Two flat reports on the same world: it doesn’t count a good person’s fall as ruin, and it scorns everyone who has nothing.
props.quote: The world does not count it ruin … Everyone scorns those who have nothing

props.why: Everyone scorns those who have nothing, yet the world is also said to count no lack as poverty except a lack of understanding.
props.quote: Everyone scorns those who have nothing … The world does not count any other lack as poverty

props.why: Drive comes because fate is bringing wealth, or prosperity comes because someone’s drive never wavers: each makes the other’s effect its cause.
props.quote: The fate that brings you wealth also brings the drive to work … Prosperity asks the way and goes by itself to someone whose drive never wavers

props.why: Someone living home life rightly gains nothing from an outside path, yet you are also told to renounce while you can, for many things are yours then.
props.quote: what would you gain by going off on some outside path? … renounce while you can

props.why: Those who harm you are to be shamed with good and let go, yet those who despise you are to be kept laughing while the friendship dies within.
props.quote: do them such good that they are ashamed … make them laugh, and within that friendship hold them so that it dies

props.why: Don’t take another life even to save your own, yet a ruler who punishes the wicked with death is likened to someone pulling weeds from a green crop.
props.quote: don’t do what takes another sweet life … A ruler who punishes the wicked with death is like someone pulling weeds from a green crop

props.why: Saying you will think after you commit is a mistake, yet those who strive without delay for their family are promised success without planning.
props.quote: To say you will think after you have committed is a mistake … success comes of itself, without planning

props.why: Desire as tall as a palmyra leaves no room for a millet seed of sulking, yet desire without sulks is like fruit too ripe or too green.
props.quote: you must not sulk even by a millet seed … Without the deep sulk and the light one, desire is like a fruit too ripe and a fruit too green

props.why: When your means shrink you must stand tall, yet those raising a family are warned that thinking of their pride will ruin it.
props.quote: When your means shrink, stand tall … Be idle and think of your pride, and it is ruined

props.why: However much you study, the understanding you were born with wins out, yet understanding is also said to flow as far as you learn.
props.quote: the understanding you were born with still wins out … People’s understanding flows as far as they learn

props.why: Deeds don’t touch those devoted to the true praise of the Lord, yet your own deed is said never to go away, but to follow you and kill.
props.quote: do not touch those devoted to the true praise of the Lord … The enemy that is your own deed never goes away

props.why: Many who didn’t know their strength broke halfway, yet you are told never to call a task too hard, because effort will give you greatness.
props.quote: set out on a surge of zeal and broke halfway … Don’t lose heart and say “This is too hard.”

props.why: Understanding is living as the world lives, yet those called the ocean of worth will not shift, even if the age itself does.
props.quote: However the world lives, understanding is living that way with the world … Even if the age itself shifts, those called the ocean of worth will not shift

props.why: A spear that missed an elephant beats an arrow that hit a hare, yet whoever won’t take the small prize of an easy fight will never win glory.
props.quote: Better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that hit a hare … If you won’t take the small prize of fighting an unlearned man, glory will never come to you

props.why: Puts a condition on the praise of learning as the great wealth that can’t be destroyed: without worship, it asks, what use is it?
props.quote: What use is learning to those who won’t worship … Learning is the great wealth that can’t be destroyed

props.why: Being without stain in your mind sounds like your own affair, but a pure mind is said to depend on pure company.
props.quote: A pure mind and pure deeds both depend on pure company … To be without stain in your mind is all of righteousness

props.why: Sets a limit on punishing the wicked like pulling weeds: a ruler must look into the wrong fairly and punish to fit it.
props.quote: looks into a wrong fairly and punishes to fit it … A ruler who punishes the wicked with death

props.why: Conditions the rule against opposing the strong: even the weak grow strong and win, if they know the place and guard themselves.
props.quote: Even the weak grow strong and win, if they know the place … Keep from opposing the strong

props.why: Softens the flat denial that the envious gain: a crooked heart does sometimes prosper, and that gives you something to think about.
props.quote: When a crooked heart prospers … the envious have no gain

props.why: Courtesy of the tongue holds in both: no evil word even by a slip, no discourtesy even in enmity.
props.quote: can’t say evil things with their mouths, even by a slip … stay courteous, even in enmity

props.why: Both lift the shame from falling low on one condition: that you stay in the good, or have the strength called worth.
props.quote: does not count it ruin when someone who stays in the middle and in the good falls low … Having nothing is no disgrace, if you have the strength called worth

props.why: Both redefine poverty: to have plenty and turn a guest away is the real poverty, and the deepest kind.
props.quote: Poverty amid plenty is the folly of neglecting guests … The deepest poverty is to turn a guest away

props.why: The goad and the tortoise drawing in its limbs make one point: whoever masters the five senses lays up what is to come.
props.quote: guards the five senses with the goad called firmness … draw in the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs

props.why: Both single out speech as the thing above all to guard, because suffering, and even ruin, ride on its slips.
props.quote: Whatever else you fail to guard, guard your tongue … guard carefully against any slip in your speech

props.why: Both set sparing life above any gain: a thousand sacrifices are worth less than not killing, and gain that comes from killing is the lowest thing.
props.quote: Better than pouring offerings into a thousand sacrifices is not to take one creature’s life and eat it … gain that comes from killing is the lowest thing

props.why: He and she say the same thing of desire: it is a fire that burns when you move away, which no real fire can do.
props.quote: It burns when you move away and cools when you come near … Can it burn when you leave it, as the sickness of desire does?

props.why: The same moment told from each side: she barely moved from his embrace, he barely loosened it, and pallor came at once.
props.quote: I lay holding him and shifted a little … When I loosened my arms in our embrace

props.why: Desire beats toddy in both for the same reason: merely thinking of it brings joy, and that is more than toddy can do.
props.quote: even thinking of it brings a great joy that doesn’t fade … To be drunk at a thought

props.why: Both are her own scolding of her heart: suffering over a man who has no love for you is foolish, as vain as filling in the sea.
props.quote: Fill in the sea instead … He has no love for you, yet you go on suffering. That is foolishness, my heart

props.why: Her heart is chided in both for the same disloyalty: it runs to the man who chose to leave and neglect her.
props.quote: you go after the one who left … Even when you see he isn’t drawn to us, my heart, you go to him

props.why: Both make the friend who can rebuke you the one to seek, whether as protection from ruin or as a check when you stray.
props.quote: If you keep companions who will rebuke you … Choose with care friends who, when you go wrong, can speak until you weep, rebuke you

props.why: Both give one rule for choosing what to do: turn down any undertaking that will not bring you real good.
props.quote: Don’t set your heart on deeds that bring no good … keep away from work that doesn’t bring good along with fame

props.why: Both warn off the same folly of taking on the mighty, which one simply forbids and the other calls beckoning to Death.
props.quote: Keep from opposing the strong … For the powerless to harm the powerful is like beckoning Death with your hand

props.why: Both stay the hand by the same means: before you hurt another, remember how that hurt feels to you.
props.quote: think of yourself before those stronger … What you know to be painful, you must not do to anyone else

props.why: Both go past forgiving to forgetting: the best thing to do with an injury is to let it slip from memory.
props.quote: It is good to forget what is not good, that very day … Forgetting it is better still

props.why: Almost word for word: understanding is seeing the reality, in every thing and from every mouth.
props.quote: understanding is seeing the reality in it … understanding is seeing the reality in it

props.why: Both define the able mind by the same double skill: making yourself heard, and catching what others really mean.
props.quote: saying things so that they go home and are easy to grasp, and seeing the subtle meaning in what others say … To speak so that others want to hear, and to take what is useful from what others say

props.why: What hurts her in both is not her own wasting but that people blame him for it.
props.quote: if people don’t spread it about that the one who won me is unkind … I ache to hear him called cruel

props.why: Both put real standing above outward rank: conduct makes a noble family in one, and sitting high makes no one high in the other.
props.quote: Good conduct is noble family … Those who aren’t high aren’t high, even sitting high

props.why: Both count winning over those not with you as sound policy, one urging haste and the other saying the world rests in such greatness.
props.quote: Be quicker to win over those not with you … one whose nature is to make friends of enemies

props.why: Both move the danger from the open enemy to the one who comes smiling as a friend.
props.quote: Fear the deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within … Fear the company of enemies who are like kin

props.why: Both treat moving in step with the world as the test of understanding, which those who never learn it lack, however much else they learn.
props.quote: Those who don’t learn to move in step with the world … understanding is living that way with the world

props.why: Both show gain unhinging a small mind: the fool is a madman getting drunk, and distinction in the unworthy turns to nothing but excess.
props.quote: it is like a madman getting drunk … when it falls to the unworthy, turns to nothing but excess

props.why: Loss will always come, whatever your heart does, yet ruin is said to be rare for anyone who doesn’t stray aside to do evil.
props.quote: Loss and gain will always come … ruin is rare for anyone who doesn’t stray aside to do evil

props.why: Those who punish a wrong count for nothing and those who bear it are kept like gold, yet those who don’t crush their foes’ pride won’t live to draw breath.
props.quote: Those who bear it are wrapped up and kept like gold … Those who fail to crush the pride of their foes surely won’t live

props.why: Smiling falsely to a face while ruining behind the back is worse than doing wrong, yet it is the advice for those who make much of you and despise you.
props.quote: to ruin someone behind their back and smile falsely to their face … make them laugh, and within that friendship hold them so that it dies

props.why: Taking is bad even if it were a good road, yet to beg from those who hide nothing is called like giving.
props.quote: Even if it were a good road, taking is bad … Begging is like giving

props.why: A lie counts as truthfulness if it brings good, yet what the worthy condemn stays forbidden even when the mother who bore you goes hungry.
props.quote: Even a lie counts as truthfulness, if it brings good with no fault in it … Even if you see the mother who bore you go hungry, don’t do what the worthy condemn

props.why: Killing brings every wrong with it, says one; in the other, the many his lord has killed, now standing in stone, are a warrior’s boast.
props.quote: Killing brings with it every action of the other kind … Many have stood before him, and now they stand in stone

props.why: The understanding you were born with wins out over all your study, yet people’s understanding is also said to take on the nature of their company.
props.quote: the understanding you were born with still wins out … People’s understanding takes on the nature of their company

props.why: What fate denies won’t stay however you guard it, yet acting in step with the season is a rope that ties good fortune down.
props.quote: What isn’t yours by fate won’t stay, however hard you guard it … a rope that ties good fortune down so that it can’t leave

props.why: Fate gets there first even as you plan around it, yet those who plan are said to get just what they planned, if they are firm.
props.quote: Even as you plan a way around it, it gets there first … Those who plan will get what they planned, just as they planned it, if they are firm

props.why: Climbing past the tip of a branch costs your life, yet all your thoughts are to be of rising higher, since even failing has the nature of not failing.
props.quote: Those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and try to go further will lose their life … Let all your thoughts be of rising higher

props.why: Full desire leaves no room for a millet seed of sulking, yet sulking is called the joy of desire.
props.quote: you must not sulk even by a millet seed … Sulking is the joy of desire

props.why: Patience may keep your integrity with you, but holding back anger only counts where the anger could take effect.
props.quote: Whoever holds back anger where it can take effect truly holds it back … guard your patience and live by it

props.why: Striving may see the back of fate, but only if it is made the right way: effort that isn’t will crack, however many stand guard.
props.quote: Effort not made the right way will crack … Those who strive without faltering and without delay will see the back of fate itself

props.why: A fortress serves those who fear and look after themselves, but for those who are only afraid there is no fort at all.
props.quote: There is no fort for those who are afraid … of value to those who fear and look after themselves

props.why: Punishing wrongdoing is no stain on a ruler and is his work, but he must look into the wrong fairly and punish to fit it.
props.quote: looks into a wrong fairly and punishes to fit it … punish wrongdoing is no stain on a ruler

props.why: Living up to what you have learned isn’t the end of it: even when you know the methods, you must know the nature of the world before you act.
props.quote: Even when you know the methods, know the nature of the world and then act … Once you have learned it, live up to it

props.why: Gaining renown is a duty, but not at any price: those who want glory with strength of character won’t do anything unworthy even for it.
props.quote: won’t do anything unworthy, even for glory … it is a disgrace for everyone on earth not to gain the legacy called renown

props.why: Having no craving is no guarantee against suffering: if those who plough fold their hands, even those who have given up all desire can’t stand firm.
props.quote: If those who plough fold their hands, even those who say they have given up all desire can’t stand firm … Those without craving have no suffering

props.why: A quarrel may be sweeter than making love, but only in the right amount: drawn out, a sulk is like a little too much salt.
props.quote: A sulk is like the right amount of salt. Drawing it out is like a little too much … a quarrel is sweeter than making love

props.why: Greatness is defined the same way in both: the great are those who do what is hard to do.
props.quote: Those who do what is hard to do are great … The great will carry out hard deeds

props.why: Do good now, because death will not wait: the day of death in one, the hiccup in the throat in the other.
props.quote: Don’t say “I’ll see to it some other day.” … Before your tongue is stilled and the hiccup rises, rush to do good deeds

props.why: Wealth guarded and never used comes to nothing: the hoarder ends with nothing to hold on to, or as a dead man beside it.
props.quote: After anxious guarding they will say “We have nothing to hold on to” … He stores up great heaps of wealth and doesn’t eat from it. He is a dead man

props.why: Turn down wealth that costs you your integrity, whatever profit it offers: honest poverty is far better.
props.quote: let go at once of gain that comes from leaving the middle … Better the deep poverty of the worthy than prosperity gained by wearing disgrace

props.why: Envy and prosperity never meet, stated once as a rule and once as what has never yet happened.
props.quote: the envious have no gain … No one has grown great through envy

props.why: Learning doesn’t cure folly: much learning can leave you without understanding, and the greatest fool of all is a teacher with no self-control.
props.quote: may learn much, but they are still without understanding … No one is a greater fool than someone who studies, understands, teaches others, and still has no self-control

props.why: Worth is the way to beat an enemy: defeat those who wrong you by your own worth, and bowing is the weapon the worthy use to turn enemies around.
props.quote: Defeat by your own worth those who wrong you … That is the weapon the worthy use to turn enemies around

props.why: Goodness outlasts the means for it: those who know their duty won’t slacken in helping, and old families keep their good nature as their giving shrinks.
props.quote: Even when they have little room to give, those who know their duty won’t slacken in helping others … Even when what they have to give has shrunk, those of an old family don’t part from their good nature

props.why: Being easy to reach decides how a ruler stands: with it his land is praised above all others, without it he falls by himself.
props.quote: If a ruler is easy to see and not harsh in speech, his land will be praised above all others … A ruler who isn’t easy to reach, and doesn’t look into things and give justice, will sink low and fall by himself

props.why: A ruler lasts by bearing what stings: the world rests under one who bears bitter words, and one with no one to rebuke him falls.
props.quote: a ruler with the character to bear words bitter to his ears … A ruler with no one to rebuke him has no protection

props.why: One rule of action stated twice: weigh the cost, the obstacles and the gain to come, and only then act.
